item.title: A Review of the AI Automation Tool Midscene.js
item.description:
Introduction

AI has been working its way ever more deeply into our day-to-day jobs. In the field of software testing, new AI-related testing tools and methods are emerging one after another. Previously we introduced a case of AI-driven testing combined with an mcp server; in this article we will introduce a domestically developed AI testing tool that has recently come to prominence, Midscene.js.

Introduction to Midscene.js

MidScene.js is an open-source AI automation testing tool released by the web-infra team at ByteDance. Built on multimodal large models, it understands our natural-language instructions through intelligent visual parsing of the page and then carries out automated operations. It can significantly reduce the complexity of writing automated test scripts, adapt better to changes in page structure and elements, and greatly improve the stability of automated test scripts.

Official website: https://midscenejs.com/

How Midscene Works

Unlike the mcp server we discussed earlier, which used a general-purpose large model to understand the page and extended capabilities by calling local tools, Midscene uses multimodal large models such as ChatGPT-4o, qwen-vl, and ByteDance’s UI-TARS-that is, large models that support visual input-to understand the page, which is much closer to the way we actually perform functional testing.

MidScene first captures the current page screenshot along with detailed page structure information, then submits them together with the user instruction to the large model, which determines the location of the page control to be operated and decides the next action.

Take entering “Today I will learn Playwright” into the task box on a to-do page as an example:

MidScene’s internal operations are roughly as follows:

  1. Get the user instruction “Enter Learning Playwright in the task box and press Enter”
  2. MidScene takes a screenshot and obtains the overall element structure of the page
  3. Submit it to the large model to extract page features
  4. Obtain the large model’s analysis result and determine the next operation type (Tap) and the specific position (coordinates) of the control
  5. Plan the next operation
  6. Complete the execution

Choosing a Large Model

From the analysis of Midscene’s principles above, MidScene mainly relies on the following capabilities of multimodal large models

  1. The ability to understand screenshots and  plan  operation steps.
  2. The ability to give the coordinate information of a specified element (Visual Grounding).

The large models that support the above capabilities, as currently listed on the official site, include the following:

  • OPENAI GPT-4o
  • Alibaba Qwen-2.5-VL
  • ByteDance UI-TARS
  • ByteDance Volcano Engine Doubao-1.5-thinking-vision-pro
  • Google Gemini-2.5-Pro

In terms of how it works, information such as screenshots and page structure has to be supplied to the large model, so the token consumption is fairly considerable. According to the official assessment, each operation usually consumes at least several thousand tokens. Among them, the model with the best cost-performance ratio recommended by the official team is QWen-VL.

Using the Chrome Extension

The no-code Chrome extension approach can help us quickly understand how MidScene is applied.

You can install it directly from the Chrome Web Store Midscene Extension

Configuring the Large Model

After enabling the extension, you need to configure the large model to use. Here we use the Alibaba Qwen multimodal model qwen-vl-max-latest, which consumes relatively few tokens; you can apply for the corresponding API Key through the Alibaba Cloud Bailian platform, and applications currently come with a free quota of 1 million tokens.

After the application is complete, configure the corresponding large model parameters in the extension’s model settings screen; the Qwen model requires the following four parameters

1
2
3
4

OPENAI_BASE_URL="https://dashscope.aliyuncs.com/compatible-mode/v1"
OPENAI_API_KEY="sk- your API KEY"
MIDSCENE_MODEL_NAME="qwen-vl-max-latest"
MIDSCENE_USE_QWEN_VL=1

Operating the Browser

Next you can experience Midscene’s control of the browser in the extension interface. It mainly supports four behaviors:

  • Action: Corresponds to AI-planned operations; Midscene automatically plans the operation steps and executes them. It is smarter but slower, and the results depend on the quality of the large model.
  • Query: Extracts data directly from the UI and, with the reasoning ability of multimodal AI, achieves intelligent extraction
  • Assert: Describes an assertion condition in natural language and lets the AI judge whether the condition is true
  • Tap: Corresponds to an immediate page-click operation; Midscene executes it directly, and the large model only handles low-level tasks such as element locating. It is more efficient and is suitable when the operation to perform is already determined

We can enter prompt instructions using AI prompts close to natural language; for different behavior modes, the extension drives the browser to perform different operations and reports the results.

The concrete execution process can also be seen in the video demo below.

Script Integration

Besides calling Midscene through the browser extension, the more recommended approach is to integrate Midscene capabilities through test framework scripts.

With script integration, you also need to configure the relevant model call parameters, the same variable values configured in the extension, except that the relevant variables need to be set as system environment variables

npm install @midscene/web --save-dev

Visual Result Report

The report is one of Midscene’s highlights. Through it you can replay the entire execution process, with detailed display of the AI’s spatial judgment process and concrete operation details, making it easy to debug and optimize scripts.

YAML File-Driven

Besides integration through test framework scripts, Midscene also supports writing test scripts directly with YAML files, enabling no-code script driving, similar to the keyword-driven approach of traditional automation.

In essence, this approach still converts the corresponding keywords into the relevant APIs supported by Midscene for driving.

To run YAML-format scripts, you need to install Midscene’s command-line support

1

3

# Run
npx midscene ./weather.yaml

MCP Approach

Beyond the methods above, Midscene also offers a way to act as a local MCP server. This approach essentially wraps MidScene’s Chrome extension as a local capability inside MCP, then drives the browser by combining a large model with the mcp server.

For an introduction to and usage of mcp server, see my earlier related article 【】

Limitations of the Current Version

Although the Midsence tool has already shown considerable potential and is still being continuously updated and iterated, it still has quite a few shortcomings in practical use, mainly in the following areas:

  • Limited interaction types: Currently only click, drag (supported only in the UI-TARS model), input, keyboard, and scroll operations are supported.
  • Stability risks: The return values of AI models cannot be guaranteed to be 100% accurate. Writing good prompts is demanding
  • Element recognition: Some large models are not very good at recognizing elements, such as interactions with iframe and canvas elements. Moreover, Chrome’s native controls like pop-up prompts and right-click menus are not yet supported.
  • Higher cost: Being based on visual recognition, token consumption is considerable, and if a paid large model is used, the cost can be high.

But these flaws do not overshadow the merits: Midscene has already taken a solid step forward in improving UI automation testing with AI capabilities! We will continue to follow its further development!

item.description:
What Is Magentic UI?

Magentic UI is an open-source Agent assistant that Microsoft released with much fanfare on May 19, and it just updated to its second version, 0.04, on the 24th

Judging from the official introduction, the goal is to build a human-centered intelligent assistant, powered at its core by several different agent systems, capable of web browsing and operation, code generation and execution, and file generation and analysis.

What mainly sets it apart from other AI browser tools is its transparent and controllable interactive interface, which supports efficient human-AI collaborative participation. The system is built on Microsoft’s agent-building framework AutoGen and is currently still at the prototype research stage.

Core features include:

🧑‍🤝‍🧑 Collaborative planning: users and the AI work together through chat and a plan editor to create and revise step-by-step execution plans.
🤝 Collaborative tasks: users can intervene in real time and guide task execution directly through the web browser or the chat interface. Magentic-UI can proactively ask for confirmation or request assistance when needed.
🛡️ Action guard: sensitive operations require explicit user approval before they can be executed.
🧠 Plan learning and retrieval: it learns from past tasks to optimize future automation workflows and saves good solutions into a plan library. Stored plans can be invoked automatically or manually in subsequent tasks.
🔀 Parallel task execution: it supports running multiple tasks in parallel, and a session status indicator shows in real time when Magentic-UI needs your input or has completed a task.

Design Architecture

The underlying system of Magentic-UI consists of a group of specialized agents adapted from AutoGen’s Magentic-One system (shown in the figure above), with each agent implementing different functions through modular collaboration:

Agent Functionality

Orchestrator

  • Functional role: the main LLM-based controlling agent, responsible for collaboratively making plans with the user, deciding when to request user feedback, and assigning subtasks to other agents.
  • Collaboration flow:
    1. Jointly create a step-by-step execution plan with the user;
    2. Dynamically determine the points where user intervention is needed;
    3. Dispatch subtasks to other agents for execution.

WebSurfer

  • Functional role: an LLM agent equipped with a web browser, supporting multi-round web interaction operations.
  • Core capabilities:
    • Following the Orchestrator’s instructions, perform operations such as clicking, typing, scrolling, and page navigation;
    • Beyond AutoGen’s multimodal web browser: adds tab management, option selection, file upload, and multimodal query support.

Coder

  • Functional role: an LLM agent equipped with a Docker code execution container.
  • Core capabilities:
    • Write and execute Python and Shell commands;
    • Feed the execution results back to the Orchestrator.

**FileSurfer

**

  • Functional role: an LLM agent integrating a Docker container with the MarkItDown package file-conversion tool.
  • Core capabilities:
    • Locate files in Magentic-UI’s controlled directory;
    • Convert files to Markdown format and support question answering over their content.

UserProxy

  • Functional role: the agent role that interacts with the system on behalf of the user.
  • Collaboration mode: the Orchestrator can delegate tasks directly to the user (rather than to other agents) to complete.

  1. Input and plan generation

    • The user triggers the flow through text/images, and the system generates an initial plan. If it fails, the user is prompted to re-enter.
    • The user iteratively refines the plan through the editing interface, and after confirmation, moves to the execution phase.

  2. Plan execution logic

    • The Orchestrator assigns tasks step by step to the corresponding agents (WebSurfer/Coder/FileSurfer) or to the user.
    • After each step is completed, the status is verified; if it fails, a decision is made on whether replanning is needed (requiring user authorization).

  3. Dynamic control and termination

    • The user can intervene at any time: pause execution, modify the plan, or terminate the flow.
    • Once all steps are completed, the final result is delivered, with transparent error feedback provided in exceptional cases.

Tool Deployment

Magentic AI is mainly developed in Python, with the web part based on FastAPI. Its AI control primarily uses Playwright to control a virtual browser inside a Docker container, which can be displayed to the user in real time. The large model behind it is mainly used through the API access methods of various open large models.

item.description:
Foreword

In several of our previous articles on AI testing, we introduced methods for achieving AI-driven test automation through several different AI browser tools, including playwright-mcp, midscene.js, and magentic ui. In fact, before these constantly emerging new tools appeared, there was an AI browser-driving tool that was released even earlier (2024.11) and is likewise still being continuously refined: Browser Use. Its implementation approach provided a great deal of reference for the related tools that came later. And after more than half a year and over 40 version iterations, the current latest version is 0.2.5, and the tool’s features have become increasingly complete.

In this article, let us take a systematic look at this AI browser.

browser-use Overview

browser-use is positioned as a simple yet powerful solution that connects different AI Agents with browsers, enabling AI-based intelligent browser automation.

It is a Python-based open-source library with over 61K stars on GitHub, which shows just how much attention it has attracted.

It mainly relies on the browser-control capabilities of Playwright/Puppeteer and the reasoning and analysis capabilities of large AI models to accomplish the shift of AI from an information assistant to an assistant that helps with execution. After it, MCP became widespread, and the subsequent variety of other AI-driven browser approaches all bear traces of the browser-use solution.

How It Works

The implementation of browser-use is, in fact, an AI Agent built with Langchain and LLM (Large Language Model) that understands web page content and further generates operation instructions. At its core, the project relies on the Playwright framework to implement browser automation operations, supports multiple browsers (such as Chromium, Firefox, etc.), and can simulate real-user behaviors like clicking, typing, and navigation.

Based on AI capabilities, the system can automatically identify interactive elements on web pages (such as buttons, input fields, etc.) and, combined with an understanding of the context, generate the corresponding interaction logic, improving automation efficiency and achieving AI-based browser intelligence.

Core Architecture Analysis

browser-use achieves deep integration between the AI Agent and the browser through a layered architecture. The main roles of the different layers of its core architecture are as follows:

Agent Layer (Decision Center)

This layer is mainly responsible for task-flow orchestration and decision-making. It manages the task flow by implementing a small state machine and interacts with the LLM (such as OpenAI) to obtain decision instructions.

Controller Layer (Instruction Converter)

This layer is responsible for translating high-level decisions into concrete browser operation instructions, supporting basic actions such as DOM operations and page navigation, and also providing management of multi-tab interaction logic.

DOM Parsing Engine

This layer performs real-time parsing of web page structure and content, including providing visual recognition capabilities (OCR support), and completes the construction of the mapping relationships for operable web page elements.

Browser Interface Layer

At this layer, the browser behavior is actually driven based on the Playwright framework. In addition to the built-in headless mode control, it can also interact with the user’s browser by specifying a browser path.

item.title: AI Testing, the Inevitable Path for Testing Teams
item.description:
This article is translated and adapted from the latest post on the well-known testing blog https://testguild.com/ and discusses a roadmap for systematically implementing and advancing AI testing within testing teams. It offers considerable reference value, so I am sharing it with you all.

AI Test Automation Is No Longer Optional

In today’s software testing field, artificial intelligence (AI) is no longer merely an option but a significant strategic advantage. AI-driven testing tools can automate everything from test case generation to test execution, enabling your team to focus on delivering higher-quality software releases.

Tal Barmeir, CEO of Blinq.io, once noted: “The role of generative AI is to help us truly solve the problem of a massive backlog of testing demand with very limited coverage—a phenomenon we see across every industry.”

AI-driven testing tools can automate the entire process from test case creation to execution and maintenance, helping testing teams:

  • Reduce test creation time by up to 80%
  • Lower test maintenance costs by 40-60%
  • Accelerate time to market through faster release cycles
  • Improve test coverage across browsers, devices, and environments
  • Free up valuable engineering resources for innovation

This guide offers a structured approach to implementing AI testing, designed to deliver both immediate benefits and long-term transformation.

Phase 1 (Days 1-15) - Define Your AI Testing Strategy

Before diving into specific tools, you first need to clarify how you want to apply AI:

  • Assistive AI: Enhances human-led testing processes.
  • Autonomous AI: Test automation driven entirely by AI, with human oversight.

“Most organizations start with assistive AI. But they soon realize its value is limited and try to move to fully AI-led. That shift requires different tools, structures, and mindsets.”

For decision-making leaders of testing teams, the key strategic decisions include:

  • Scope of automation: Is your team automating existing test cases, or allowing AI to take full charge of creating, executing, and maintaining test scripts?

  • Integration requirements: How will AI testing integrate with your existing CI/CD pipelines and development workflows?

  • Success metrics: Which KPIs will be used to measure success (such as test coverage, execution time, defect detection, and so on)?

  • Risk assessment: Which applications or features are best suited as the initial targets for AI testing implementation?

Action recommendation: Before evaluating tools, be sure to define your AI testing vision, scope, and success criteria.

Phase 2 (Days 16-30) - Redefine QA Roles and Test Inputs

AI test automation does not eliminate existing roles; rather, it transforms them.

Traditional Role AI-Augmented Role Key Responsibilities
Manual Tester Prompt Engineer Create effective test prompts, review AI-generated tests
Automation Engineer AI Testing Lead Oversee the generation, execution, and maintenance of AI tests
QA Manager AI Testing Strategist Define AI testing strategy, measure ROI, optimize processes

“People often think AI means job losses. That is not the case. What it really does is redeploy testers—manual testers become prompt engineers, and automation engineers become supervisors of AI work.”

Expand Test Input Sources

AI testing platforms can generate comprehensive test cases from a variety of inputs, including:

  • Jira tickets and user stories
  • Screen recordings of application usage
  • Natural language requirements
  • API specifications and documentation
  • Existing manual test cases

This flexibility means AI testing does not need to strictly adhere to a BDD framework or a specific test case format, making AI testing accessible to teams at every maturity level.

Phase 3 (Days 31-45) - Evaluate AI Testing Tools

Choosing the right AI testing tool requires aligning it with your infrastructure, team skills, and long-term vision.

Core Capabilities of Enterprise AI Testing Platforms

  • Open-source test code generation: Generates maintainable code in standard frameworks (such as Playwright, Selenium, and so on).
  • Self-healing capability: Automatically adapts to user interface (UI) changes without human intervention.
  • Comprehensive test support: Covers functional, visual, performance, and security testing.
  • Enterprise integration: Works with your CI/CD pipelines, test management, and defect tracking systems.
  • Cross-platform testing: Supports web, mobile, API, and enterprise applications (such as Salesforce, SAP, and so on).
  • Visual testing: AI-driven visual comparison and anomaly detection.
  • Flaky test management: Automatically identifies and resolves inconsistent tests.

“Even if you stop using a particular vendor, you still have a code project you can maintain. No black box, no vendor lock-in.”

Decision framework: Evaluate tools against your specific needs, existing infrastructure, and team capabilities. Give priority to platforms that generate standard, maintainable test code rather than proprietary formats.

Phase 4 (Days 46-60) - Train for New AI-Augmented Testing Roles

Introducing AI into test automation brings new AI capabilities and responsibilities, elevating the role of the QA team.

Key Skills for the AI Testing Era

  • Prompt engineering: Creating effective test prompts to generate comprehensive test coverage.
  • AI test review: Evaluating and refining AI-generated test scripts.
  • Test maintenance management: Overseeing self-healing capabilities and test stability.
  • Test prioritization: Determining which tests deliver the highest value in each release.
  • Exploratory testing: Concentrating human creativity on edge cases and complex scenarios.

“The old skills were scripting and debugging. The new skills? Writing prompts, reviewing AI suggestions, and managing code at scale.”

Training Resources for the QA Team:

  • Internal workshops on AI testing concepts and prompt engineering.
  • Vendor-provided training on specific AI testing platforms.
  • Hands-on practice in real application testing scenarios.
  • Cross-training between manual and automation testers.

Leadership focus: Encourage experimentation and create a learning environment where the team can develop AI testing expertise through real-world application.

Phase 5 (Days 61-75) - Pilot and Expand AI Testing Coverage

Launch a focused pilot project using 10-20 test scenarios to achieve fast, measurable impact and build confidence in AI testing capabilities.

Ideal Pilot Project Characteristics:

  • An application of moderate complexity with a stable UI.
  • Existing manual test cases for comparison.
  • A regular release cadence to demonstrate CI/CD integration.
  • A mix of regression, functional, and visual testing needs.
  • Stakeholders who are open to innovation and process change.

Implementation Checklist:

  • Select the pilot application and define the test scope.
  • Configure the AI testing tool and integrate with CI/CD.
  • Create initial test prompts and generate baseline tests.
  • Execute tests across multiple environments.
  • Measure results against traditional testing methods.
  • Document lessons learned and optimization opportunities.

This phase is ideal for expanding test coverage across browsers, devices, and languages—leveraging the multilingual capabilities of AI models to efficiently test international applications.

Phase 6 (Days 76-90) - Measure KPIs and Optimize

Track key performance indicators (KPIs) to quantify the impact of AI testing implementation and uncover optimization opportunities.

Key AI Testing Metrics:

  • Release time: Reduction in overall test cycle time.
  • Test coverage: Increase in functional and platform coverage.
  • Maintenance effort: Reduction in test script maintenance time.
  • Defect detection: Increase in the defect identification rate.
  • Resource utilization: The QA team shifting focus to higher-value activities.

“Most leaders think AI testing is about cutting costs. But the biggest ROI is actually faster time to market.”

Continuous Improvement Framework:

  • Review AI testing performance and accuracy weekly.
  • Refine prompts based on test results and missed scenarios.
  • Extend AI testing to other applications and test types.
  • Document best practices and share them across teams.
  • Establish an AI testing center of excellence.

These insights will support your team in making data-driven decisions about test coverage, release readiness, and quality improvement.

Summary - Your 90-Day AI Testing Implementation Roadmap

Phase Timeline Focus Key Deliverables
1 Days 1-15 Strategy definition AI testing vision, implementation approach, success metrics
2 Days 16-30 Role transformation Updated team structure, skill requirements, input sources
3 Days 31-45 Tool selection AI testing platform evaluation, selection criteria, proof of concept
4 Days 46-60 Team training Skill development plan, training resources, knowledge sharing
5 Days 61-75 Pilot implementation Initial AI test suite, CI/CD integration, baseline metrics
6 Days 76-90 Measurement and optimization Performance analysis, optimization plan, scaling strategy

The Future of QA - AI-Driven Testing Leadership

With the right AI testing strategy, your QA organization will not only keep pace with the industry but will lead the transformation toward faster, more reliable software delivery. You are not merely automating tests; you are empowering your team to enhance and streamline the entire testing lifecycle, delivering higher-quality software at unprecedented speed while reducing risk and technical debt. Embrace AI testing now, and you will position your organization at the forefront of quality engineering, creating a sustainable competitive advantage through superior software quality and accelerated innovation.

item.description:
Preface

MCP protocol is an open protocol for AI capabilities launched in November 2024 by the AI company Anthropic (the parent company of Claude), aimed at standardizing the interaction interface between large language models (LLMs) and external data sources and tools. Its core design goals:

  • Decoupling and standardization — shifting the integration of LLMs with external systems from custom development to universal connections based on a unified protocol, similar to the USB-C interface in hardware.
  • Decentralization — by allowing developers to build their own MCP Servers, distributing AI capabilities and avoiding a single vendor’s monopoly on knowledge and services.
  • Security and control — ensuring data privacy and operational safety through permission verification and localized deployment.

And MCP Server is the key component of MCP, providing the following three functions:

  • Resources — file-like data that can be read by clients, such as API responses or file contents.
  • Tools — functions that can be called by the LLM (requiring user approval).
  • Prompts — pre-written templates that help users accomplish specific tasks.

Through these capabilities, MCP Server can provide AI applications with richer context and the ability to operate on private data or specific applications, thereby enhancing the usefulness of LLMs.

In the previous article 【】, we gained a basic understanding of MCP Server, provided a basic example of querying the local desktop, and used the AI editor Cursor to invoke this MCP server.

Microsoft Officially Releases Playwright-mcp

Among the many current applications of MCP Server, orchestrating browser operations is an extremely high-frequency scenario. Based on Playwright, this rising new browser tool, third parties have already taken the lead in releasing an MCP Server.

And now, Microsoft has finally officially released Playwright-mcp, which can be used seamlessly with VS Code Copilot.

Playwright-mcp Deployment

Because Playwright-mcp has just been released, its integration in VS Code is currently mainly in the preview edition, VS Code Insiders. So we can first download VS Code Insiders from the official VS Code website.

After installing VS Code Insiders, on the GitHub project homepage, simply click the corresponding button to install it.

After opening VS Code, select install server; this will automatically configure the MCP server’s configuration file. Click start to run the MCP server, and with that the deployment is actually complete.

Click the tools button shown in the Copilot dialog box to see the currently integrated tools, which mainly correspond to Playwright’s 15 main operation behaviors.

Complete Browser Operations and Verification with Playwright-mcp Without Writing Code

Let’s take a look at the results below.

Open Copilot and enter the instruction:

Navigate to https://www.saucedemo.com, log in with the account standard_user and the password secret_sauce, confirm the login succeeds, and verify the product page displays correctly

Continue the execution and obtain the result — the test case ran successfully.

As you can see, here we did not write any code, yet used Playwright’s MCP to complete the execution of the login test case.

Of course, in real work, the integration of the MCP server is more about giving us greater convenience in calling the browser to carry out task execution!

Based on MCP Server, I believe there are still more and richer practices that can help us!

item.title: The Next Stop for AI - MCP Server
item.description:
Introduction

In 2025, as AI technology evolves at breakneck speed, the limitations of large models are becoming increasingly apparent; they possess powerful reasoning capabilities, yet struggle to directly access private data or invoke external tools. This pain point has given rise to a revolutionary technology — MCP (Model Context Protocol) — and MCP Server, its core component, is fast becoming the next big thing in the AI industry. This article takes a deep dive into the technical essence and industry value of MCP Server, and explores its application prospects through real-world cases.

Part One - What Is MCP? The Past and Present of MCP

1. The Definition and Design Goals of MCP

MCP is an open protocol introduced by the AI company Anthropic (the parent company of Claude) in November 2024, designed to standardize the interaction interface between large language models (LLMs) and external data sources and tools. Its core design goals:

  • Decoupling and Standardization: Transforming the integration of LLMs with external systems from custom development into universal connections based on a unified protocol, similar to the USB-C interface in hardware.
  • Decentralization: By allowing developers to build their own MCP Servers, AI capabilities are distributed, preventing a single vendor from monopolizing knowledge and services.
  • Security and Control: Ensuring data privacy and operational safety through permission verification and local deployment.

2. The Technical Evolution from Langchain to MCP

Before MCP, developers relied on middleware frameworks such as Langchain to connect LLMs with tools, but these solutions had two major bottlenecks:

  1. Fragmentation: API standards vary across vendors, making integration costly;
  2. Closedness: The plugin ecosystems of vendors such as OpenAI are confined to their own platforms, making reuse across models difficult.

Through abstraction at the protocol layer, MCP encapsulates capabilities such as tool invocation and data access into standardized interfaces, so that any LLM supporting the MCP protocol can seamlessly connect to third-party services.

3. The Current State of the MCP Ecosystem

At this stage, the MCP ecosystem has begun to take shape:

  • Support from Leading Companies: Besides Claude from the company that initiated it, OpenAI, a leader in the AI industry, as well as domestic players such as Baidu and Tencent, have all announced support for MCP
  • A Large Developer Base: Thanks to a low barrier to entry, the various publicly available MCP Servers have grown explosively; within just a few weeks, thousands of public Servers have appeared, covering areas such as databases, design tools, and payment systems.
  • Emerging Business Value: Institutions such as a16z have drawn up MCP market maps, predicting it may give rise to a “Stripe of the Agentic AI space” caliber company.

Part Two - What Does MCP Server Do? Why Might It Be the AI Industry’s Next Big Thing?

1. The Core Functions of MCP Server

An MCP Server is a concrete implementation of the MCP protocol, playing the following key roles:

  • Tool Proxy: Converting external APIs (such as GitHub and PostgreSQL) into standardized tool descriptions that LLMs can understand, for example abstracting “create a GitHub Issue” into a function call.
  • Data Gateway: Securely accessing local or cloud data, for example letting an LLM read desktop files through a file-system MCP Server.
  • Workflow Orchestration: Supporting chained calls across multiple tools, for example querying a database first and then generating a report.

2. Three Major Drivers Behind the Craze

(1) Technology Trend - From “Fat Models” to “Thin Models + Ecosystem”

Traditional “fat models” try to internalize all knowledge within their parameters, resulting in high training costs and poor timeliness. Under the MCP architecture, LLMs focus on language understanding, while knowledge extension and tool invocation are handled by the MCP Server network, forming a new paradigm of “thin models + distributed capabilities”.

(2) Economic Model - The AI-ification of the Creator Economy

MCP allows individual developers to earn revenue shares by building MCP Servers (such as a bird knowledge base), forming a decentralized knowledge economy network. For example, OpenMCP.Network, built on Ethereum, can automatically settle call volumes through smart contracts.

(3) Industry Demand - The Rigid Need for Private Enterprise AI Deployment

Enterprises can use MCP Servers to securely expose internal systems (such as CRM and ERP) to LLMs without uploading sensitive data to the cloud. Companies such as NineData have launched database MCP Server solutions that support localized data management.

Part Three - As Software Testing Professionals, How Do We Apply MCP Server?

1. MCP-ifying Testing Scenarios

(1) Simulating External Dependencies

By building Mock MCP Servers to replace dependencies such as real payment and third-party APIs, test environment isolation is achieved. For example, simulating the Alipay interface returning an abnormal response to verify the system’s fault tolerance.

(2) Data-Driven Testing

Store test cases in a database or file, and have the MCP Server read and execute them dynamically. For example:

1
2
3
4

@mcp.tool()
def load_test_cases():
 """Load JSON-format test cases from the specified directory"""
 return json.load(open("test_cases.json"))

The test framework can automatically obtain the cases and generate test reports.

(3) AI-Assisted Testing

Use LLMs to invoke testing tools through MCP Servers, for example:

  • Automatic Test Script Generation: Generating Selenium code from requirement descriptions;
  • Intelligent Log Analysis: Locating the root causes of defects with an ELK Stack MCP Server.

2. Skill Upgrade Suggestions for Testing Professionals

  • Master MCP Server Development: Learn the Python/TypeScript MCP SDKs to build customized testing tools.
  • Get Familiar with the Mainstream MCP Ecosystem: Follow the Awesome MCP Servers list on GitHub to learn about testing-related services (such as PostgreSQL and JIRA integrations).

Part Four - A Simple MCP Server Implementation Case - A Desktop File Query Service

1. Environment Setup

  • Install the Python MCP SDK: pip install mcp
  • Create a project directory: mkdir mcp-demo && cd mcp-demo

2. Code Implementation 

 1

 3
 4
 5
 6
 7
 8

10
11
12

from mcp.server.fastmcp import FastMCP
import os

mcp = FastMCP()

@mcp.tool()
def list_desktop_files():
 """Get the list of files on the current user's desktop"""
 return os.listdir(os.path.expanduser("~/Desktop"))

if __name__ == "__main__":
 mcp.run(transport='stdio')

This code defines an MCP Server that provides the list_desktop_files tool, allowing an LLM to query the user’s desktop files.

3. Client Configuration and Testing

Add the configuration to mcp.json in the Cursor editor:

1
2
3
4
5
6
7

{
 "mcpServers": {
 "desktop": {
 "command": "python server.py"
 }
 }
}

After starting the service, we can directly ask, “What files are on my desktop?” Cursor will invoke the service through the MCP protocol, return a list of files currently on my desktop, and classify them by type.

Conclusion

MCP Server is reshaping the way AI interacts with the physical world. For developers, it is a sharp tool for lowering integration costs; for enterprises, it is the key to unlocking the value of data; for testing professionals, it is a new engine for the evolution of automation. Although the ecosystem is still in its early days, its standardized, decentralized design philosophy has already pointed the way to the next stop for the AI industry. As Anthropic put it, “MCP is not the destination, but the starting point of the Agentic AI era.”

item.title: Software Testing in the AI Era - Assistant or Adversary?
item.description:
In the present era, the AI wave is sweeping in, and “the future is already here” is no longer an empty slogan. AI-related topics and discussions have become the sure-fire “traffic magnet” of the tech world; from autonomous driving to intelligent customer service, every industry seems eager to ride this wave of AI hype.

But as testing professionals, when we face the rapid development of AI, what we care about most is probably this: What can AI actually do in software testing? Can it really help us improve output and efficiency? Or, as it evolves, will AI completely replace testing roles?

In this article, let us explore this topic.

The Role of AI in the Different Stages of Software Testing

AI testing, when it comes down to it, is about having AI take on part of, assist with, or enhance the original testing work. In other words, AI itself does not change the underlying laws of the software testing lifecycle within software development.

Therefore, we can look at what role AI can play from the perspective of the different stages of the software testing lifecycle and the scope of testing responsibilities.

Requirements Analysis Stage

At this stage, we can use AI’s natural language processing technology to sort out the original requirements documents and produce analysis results including business flowcharts, operation flowcharts, and data flow diagrams.

At the same time, we can combine more relevant local data — such as historical bug data, test logs, and project data — to identify testing priorities, build risk models, and detect risks. Based on these analysis results, we can then help formulate a more reasonable test plan.

Test Case Design Stage

During the software design and development phase, testers usually complete test design in parallel. At this stage, we can leverage AI to help us generate test cases based on the requirements documents and the results of the requirements analysis phase. With AI, we can produce more and fuller positive and negative cases as well as a variety of boundary conditions to expand coverage.

Test Preparation Stage

At this stage, the main work is setting up and deploying the test environment. We can use AI capabilities combined with a CI platform to achieve intelligent management of test servers and database environments, as well as the dynamic allocation of resources.

Test Execution Stage

During the execution stage, we can dynamically adjust the test order based on factors such as various risk assessments, dependencies, and business impact, prioritizing coverage of higher-risk modules so as to expose defects as early as possible.

In addition, AI can enhance capabilities such as log analysis and image comparison, improving our test execution efficiency and defect detection ability.

Test Reporting Stage

In the closing part of testing, using AI to perform comprehensive analysis of various process data can help us produce multi-dimensional test reports, providing project decision-makers with a structured analysis of testing status.

How AI Empowers Software Testing at This Stage

The current development of AI can already provide more support in many typical testing scenarios. The following outlines some typical scenarios that can be empowered by AI:

  • Intelligent Data Generation - Create diverse datasets covering common scenarios and edge cases
  • Test Automation - Automatically adapt to UI changes to keep automation scripts stable
  • Precise Regression Testing - Intelligently select related test cases based on code changes
  • Process Cloning - Learn testing workflows and then automatically execute similar processes
  • Dynamic Waiting Mechanism - Intelligently judge page load status before performing actions
  • Intelligent Log Analysis - Analyze and identify potential problem patterns in error logs
  • Load / Performance Testing - Simulate real user behavior and diagnose performance bottlenecks
  • Continuous Test Monitoring - Monitor application status in real time and alert on anomalies
  • Exploratory Testing Support - Provide intelligent suggestions during exploratory testing
  • Predictive Analysis - Predict release risks based on historical data

The Advantages of Introducing AI

AI can keep learning, training, and improving continuously, so after introducing AI, we can build advantages across many of the following aspects:

  • Cost Optimization - Reduce labor costs, optimize resource allocation, and speed up time to market
  • Stable and Reliable - Ensure standardized test execution and result consistency
  • Early Defect Screening - Expose problems early and shorten the fix cycle
  • Fast Feedback - Run tests in parallel across multiple environments to shorten the feedback loop
  • High-Quality Cases - Automatically generate diverse cases such as unit tests, regression tests, and API tests

Significant Challenges Still Remain in Applying AI

Artificial Intelligence or “Artificial Stupidity”?

If AI’s training data is biased, the results can be so absurd that they make you question reality. If the training outcome of AI is not ideal, then applying AI may not only fail to improve efficiency, but also waste a large amount of extra resources correcting its execution results.

Data Dependency Syndrome

AI’s high demands for quality training data and various parameter adjustments often impose significant constraints on real-world deployment in specific industries.

Maintenance Costs Are Higher Than You Think

Beyond the investment in data resources, training models on local datasets also requires a great deal of time and money, including equipment resources, which are a considerable expense. In addition, the current shortage of AI talent makes the labor cost of AI applications much higher.

Experience and Intuition Are Things AI Can Never Learn

Veteran testers with rich experience can sniff out hidden defects in a product from all kinds of subtle clues; this “mystical,” sixth-sense-like ability is bound to be difficult for AI to replicate.

Assistant or Adversary?

“With AI developing like this, are test engineers going to lose their jobs?” There is really no need to panic!

AI is still essentially a tool. Just as test automation replaced some manual checks, it only changes parts of the way we work rather than eliminating the role altogether. Future testers will be more like an “AI Trainer + Strategy Commander” — what we actually need to do boils down to the following:

  • Teach AI to understand business logic (for example, what a “correct order status transition” is);
  • Design smarter testing strategies (for example, how to balance automation and exploratory testing);
  • Interpret AI’s results and make decisions (for example, whether a given anomaly is a bug or a false positive).

AI is like a robotic vacuum: it can help you clean the floor, but when it comes to stubborn stains (complex business scenarios) or changes in furniture layout (requirement changes), you still have to step in yourself.

Conclusion - AI Is Not the End, but a New Starting Point

The application of AI in software testing is still in its infancy. We can see its enormous potential, but it is not yet time to place full trust in it and abandon the original models. As testers, rather than worrying about “whether we will be replaced,” it is better to actively embrace change: learn some basic machine learning, get to know mainstream AI testing tools, and even take part in training your own models.

After all, in the future world of software testing, the most sought-after people will certainly not be “those who are best at clicking a mouse,” but “those who are best at working with AI”. What do you think?

Some earlier articles also discussed the development of AI. For further reading:

In the AI Era, Do Programmers Still Have a Future?

The Testing Profession and Its Future Prospects

item.title: Generating Test Scripts Automatically with DeepSeek and VS Code
item.description:
DeepSeek has been all the rage in recent days, so I gave it a try myself, and it is indeed very powerful. The AI ToolKit extension for VS Code has also integrated the DeepSeek R1 model by now, so here I would like to share my hands-on experience of using DeepSeek inside VS Code to help us complete automated test scripts.

Installing AI ToolKit and Enabling DeepSeek

Microsoft officially provides an AI-assistance extension, namely AI ToolKit for Visual Studio Code. This extension can leverage a variety of open-source or commercial large language models, and it has now integrated the DeepSeek R1 model, allowing us to conveniently use DeepSeek within VS Code to assist with our code development.

First, find AI ToolKit in the extension marketplace and complete the installation.

Once the extension is installed, on its page select the Models page in the Catalog, and use the DeepSeek-R1 model by applying the filters hosted by Github and publisher Deepseek.

AI-Assisted Script Generation

With the DeepSeek model available, we can create a new playground and let DeepSeek generate automation scripts for us. Below are the test scripts targeting saucedemo that I had DeepSeek generate.

Thinking Process

Hmm, I now need to help design an automated testing project based on pytest and Playwright, targeting the login and checkout flows of saucedemo.com, using the POM pattern, with user data stored in user.yml, and also covering exceptional scenarios. Alright, I’ll take it step by step.

First, I should determine the project structure. With the POM pattern, there are usually page objects, test cases, configuration files, data files, and so on. The directory structure might look like this:

  • tests/
    • pages/
      • login_page.py
      • inventory_page.py
      • cart_page.py
      • checkout_page.py
    • test_login.py
    • test_checkout.py
  • conftest.py
  • user.yml
  • pytest.ini

Then, the user data is stored in user.yml, which should contain different user types, such as a standard user, a locked user, a wrong password, a missing user, and so on. The test cases then need to read this data.

Next comes the implementation of the Page Object Model. Each page—such as the login page, inventory page, cart page, and checkout page—has its own class that encapsulates elements and operations. For example, LoginPage has methods for the username and password inputs, the login button, and error messages.

The test cases should use pytest’s parametrization to cover different user scenarios, such as a successful login, an invalid password, a locked user, and so on. At the same time, the checkout flow needs tests for the normal path, and possibly cases where the information is filled in incompletely.

Then consider setting up Playwright fixtures in conftest.py, such as the browser, page, and the fixtures for each page object. For example, before each test, navigate to the login page, and after login to the inventory page, so that preconditions can be handled.

As for exceptional scenarios, they include various error messages during login, and form validation during checkout, such as the first name being required. These test cases need to be written, and it must be verified that the error prompts are correct.

How should the user data be loaded? Possibly the pyYAML library can be used to read the user.yml file, which holds the data for different users. During testing, use @pytest.mark.parametrize to feed in different user data.

For example, the user data is divided into keys such as valid_users, invalid_password, and locked_user. When testing login, parametrize these cases to trigger different test cases.

When testing the checkout flow, you may need to log in first, then add a product to the cart, go to the cart, enter the checkout page, fill in the information, and complete the checkout. In this case, the normal test cases need valid data, while exceptional cases—such as leaving certain fields blank—need to verify the error prompts.

We also need to handle element selectors and Playwright’s locating methods, such as using CSS selectors or text-based locating. For example, the login page may locate the username and password inputs by id.

In addition, does the state need to be cleaned up after a test? For example, the products in the cart, or whether a logout is needed, or keeping each test case independent—fixtures may be used to ensure each one’s own state.

It may also be necessary to handle asynchronous operations, but Playwright handles waiting automatically, so no extra handling is needed for page navigation or element clicks.

Now, the concrete steps:

  1. Create the project structure and install dependencies: pytest, playwright, pyyaml.
  2. Write user.yml containing different types of user data.
  3. Implement the Page classes for each page, including element locating and operation methods.
  4. Define fixtures in conftest.py, such as initializing the page and creating instances of each page object.
  5. Write test cases, parametrize the user data, and cover both normal and exceptional flows.
  6. Handle waits and assertions in the tests to ensure elements exist or text is correct.

We need to check whether the test cases cover the following scenarios:

Login:

  • Successful login with the correct username and password.
  • An incorrect password triggers an error message.
  • A locked user cannot log in.
  • An empty username or password triggers an error.

Checkout:

  • Filling in all the information normally completes the order.
  • A missing required field (e.g., an empty first name) triggers an error.
  • The cancel-order flow.

Now, what should the structure of user.yml look like?

Possibly like this:

users: valid_user: username: standard_user password: secret_sauce invalid_password_user: username: standard_user password: wrongpass locked_user: username: locked_out_user password: secret_sauce missing_username: username: "" password: secret_sauce missing_password: username: standard_user password: ""

When testing login, parametrize these cases. For example, for valid_user, login should succeed and redirect to /inventory.html. For invalid_password, it displays Epic sadface: Username and password do not match. For a locked user, it shows Epic sadface: Sorry, this user has been locked out. A missing username or password shows the corresponding error message.

For the checkout flow, the feasible steps are:

After logging in, add a product to the cart, click the cart icon, enter the cart page, click the checkout button, fill in the information, continue, and finish.

So the test cases need to parametrize whether the information filled in is correct. For example:

Information for the normal case:

first_name: John last_name: Doe zip: 12345

For an exceptional case, such as leaving the first name blank, whether an error is shown.

When writing these tests, you need to use the page object methods to complete each step, such as adding a product, going to the cart, filling in the information, the continue button, and so on.

Potential problem areas:

Whether elements are located correctly, especially whether dynamically generated content or asynchronously loaded parts need waiting. However, Playwright has an automatic waiting mechanism, so as long as elements are selected correctly, there should be no problem.

The places that need assertions include: whether the page URL after login is correct, whether the confirmation message after the order is completed exists, and whether the error prompt displays the correct text.

For example, after a successful login it should redirect to /inventory.html; after checkout is completed it should display “Thank you for your order”.

Also, the cart may need to be cleaned up, but since each test may run independently, or each test starts a new session, this can be handled in a fixture—for example, logging in and resetting the state before each test?

Or use a beforeEach-like fixture so that each test case starts in a certain state—for example, the page after login.

In addition, testing the shopping flow requires adding products to the cart, so the inventory page class needs a method for adding a product.

Page class example:

InventoryPage can have a method for adding a certain product, such as clicking the “Add to cart” button—for example, locating the corresponding button by the product name. However, this may be rather complex; perhaps a generic method on the page would be better.

Alternatively, InventoryPage has a method add_item_to_cart(item_name) used to click the add button for the corresponding product. This requires using Playwright’s locating methods, for example:

def add_item_to_cart(self, item_name): self.page.locator(f"text={item_name}").locator(“xpath=..”).locator(“button”).click()

However, this may need to be determined based on the actual DOM structure. The inspector may be needed to examine the element structure.

For example, the structure of each product item might look like:

Sauce Labs Backpack

So, find the corresponding name element, then find the button within its parent element.

Or, a simpler approach is that each product’s “Add to cart” button has a different id, such as add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack, or another attribute. It depends on the actual structure of the site.

The page after login may have multiple products, and the add button corresponding to each product may need to be located via its text, or through other attributes.

Now, we need to actually examine the structure of saucedemo.com. Playwright’s code generation feature may be used to obtain the correct selectors.

Suppose, for example, that the id of each product’s “Add to cart” button is dynamically generated or similar—for instance, for “Sauce Labs Backpack” the corresponding button’s id might be add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack—then we can locate it directly by this id.

In that case, InventoryPage can have a method:

def add_product_to_cart(self, product_name): product_id = product_name.lower().replace(’ ‘, ‘-’) self.page.click(f"#add-to-cart-{product_id}")

Of course, this requires checking whether the actual site structure is correct.

Suppose the correct product example here is Sauce Labs Backpack and its id is indeed like this; then the method works.

Also, whether the count on the cart icon is correct—after a product is added, the cart icon shows a count of 1. When entering the cart page, whether the corresponding product is present.

Note that after each operation, a page change may require a new Page object instance. For example, after clicking the cart in InventoryPage, it navigates to CartPage, so that operation should return an instance of CartPage so that operations can continue.

Then handling the return values of methods may become an issue. For example:

The method in InventoryPage:

def go_to_cart(self): self.page.click(".shopping_cart_link") return CartPage(self.page)

Like this, each navigation action returns a new Page object.

This requires handling the return of the corresponding page object in the methods of each page.

Then comes the assembly of the test flow:

When testing checkout, there may be many steps, so a large test case needs to be written and carried out step by step:

For example:

def test_checkout_process(login_page, inventory_page, checkout_data): # Log in login_page.login(“standard_user”, “secret_sauce”) # Add a product inventory_page.add_product_to_cart(“Sauce Labs Backpack”) inventory_page.go_to_cart() # Enter the cart page and click checkout cart_page.click_checkout() # Fill in the checkout information checkout_page.fill_shipping_info(checkout_data) checkout_page.continue_to_overview() # Confirm the order checkout_page.finish_checkout() # Assert whether it succeeded assert checkout_page.get_order_confirmation() == “Thank you for your order!”

Of course, this may involve navigation across many pages, and each pair of pages needs to be connected with the corresponding methods.

As for exceptional scenarios, for example, when filling in the information, if the first name is not entered and continue is clicked, an error prompt appears.

In this case, the test case may parametrize different data, for example:

@pytest.mark.parametrize(“first_name, last_name, zip_code, error_message”, [ ("", “Doe”, “12345”, “Error: First Name is required”), (“John”, “”, “12345”, “Error: Last Name is required”), (“John”, “Doe”, “”, “Error: Postal Code is required”), ]) def test_checkout_missing_fields(…, first_name, last_name, zip_code, error_message): # Omit the corresponding field when filling in the information checkout_page.fill_shipping_info(first_name, last_name, zip_code) checkout_page.continue_to_overview() assert checkout_page.get_error_message() == error_message

It may also be necessary to consider whether the error-message element is located correctly, and whether an error prevents moving to the next step.

Now, the question may be how to organize this data and the page methods.

In addition, regarding loading the user data, the test cases need to load it from a YAML file. One possible approach is to write a fixture in conftest.py that reads the YAML data and then parametrizes the test cases.

But pytest’s parametrization may need to be handled in a specific way, possibly converting the YAML data into test parameters, or using an external data source to parametrize the tests.

For example, read all the user data from user.yml in conftest.py and create a parametrized fixture for the login tests.

Or, the data in the YAML file can be read directly in the test cases and parametrized.

For example:

import yaml

def load_users(): with open(‘user.yml’) as f: data = yaml.safe_load(f) return data[‘users’]

Then in the test case use:

@pytest.mark.parametrize(“user”, [ (“valid_user”), (“invalid_password_user”), (“locked_user”), # … other cases ], indirect=True) def test_login(login_page, user): login_page.login(user[‘username’], user[‘password’]) # assertions, etc.

However, how to convert the data into parameters may require more careful handling, such as extracting each user data item into parameters for each test instance.

A possibly better approach is to write the different user situations as separate test data items. For example, list the keys of the different user-type data, then load the corresponding parameters from the data based on these keys.

Or, when parametrizing, import all the user data as parameters.

For example:

import yaml import pytest

with open(‘user.yml’) as f: user_data = yaml.safe_load(f)[‘users’]

login_test_data = [ (user_data[‘valid_user’], True, None), # normal user, login succeeds, no error (user_data[‘invalid_password_user’], False, ‘Epic sadface: Username and password do not match’), (user_data[’locked_user’], False, ‘Epic sadface: Sorry, this user has been locked out.’), # … other cases ]

@pytest.mark.parametrize(“user, success, error_msg”, login_test_data) def test_login_user(login_page, user, success, error_msg): login_page.navigate() login_page.login(user[‘username’], user[‘password’]) if success: assert login_page.current_url == ‘https://www.saucedemo.com/inventory.html' else: assert login_page.get_error_message() == error_msg

In this case, each user data item in user.yml needs to have an error key, or the mapping of error messages needs to be handled during the preparation of the parametrization.

However, this way of passing parameters may be more flexible, allowing the expected result to be specified at the same time.

For the YAML structure, more detailed data items may be needed, with each user data item containing the expected error message.

For example, part of user.yml:

valid_user: username: standard_user password: secret_sauce expected: success: true error: null

invalid_password_user: username: standard_user password: wrong expected: success: false error: “Epic sadface: Username and password do not match”

locked_user: username: locked_out_user password: secret_sauce expected: success: false error: “Epic sadface: Sorry, this user has been locked out.”

This makes the parametrization more structured. But when writing the YAML, the expected result of each case needs to be considered.

In this way, the parameters of the test cases may be the structure read directly from the YAML, and then the test case parameters are generated by parsing the different user groups.

However, this may be somewhat complex. Another approach is to define each test case as an item in the YAML, containing the input data and the expected result.

In short, this part may require more design.

Then, regarding the Playwright fixture setup, in conftest.py you can use the fixtures provided by pytest-playwright—for example, the page fixture from the pytest-playwright plugin. However, this may require installing the pytest-playwright library and running the playwright installation step.

The dependencies to install include:

pytest-playwright playwright pyyaml

Run playwright install to install the browsers.

Then, in conftest.py, define how to initialize each page object and inject them into the test cases as fixtures.

For example:

import pytest from playwright.sync_api import Page from pages.login_page import LoginPage from pages.inventory_page import InventoryPage

Importing Other Pages

@pytest.fixture def login_page(page: Page): return LoginPage(page)

@pytest.fixture def inventory_page(page: Page): return InventoryPage(page)

And so on. In this way, if a test case needs to use a particular page object, it can simply declare the required fixture in its parameters.

For example, a test case function may receive login_page and inventory_page as parameters.

Next, examples of each Page class.

The LoginPage class looks like this:

class LoginPage: def init(self, page): self.page = page self.username_input = page.locator("#user-name") self.password_input = page.locator("#password") self.login_button = page.locator("#login-button") self.error_message = page.locator(".error-message-container")

 self.page.goto("https://www.saucedemo.com")

 self.username_input.fill(username)
 self.password_input.fill(password)
 self.login_button.click()

def get_error_message(self):
 return self.error_message.inner_text()

But in reality the selectors need to be adjusted according to the actual HTML structure of saucedemo.com. For example, the error-message element might be a div.error-message-container with a data-test=“error” attribute, whose text may be inside a child element.

For instance, on the actual site, the HTML of the error message might be:

Epic sadface: Username and password do not match any user in this service

Then, the error_message locator needs to target the text of the h3 element. Or, target the entire container and use inner_text() to get the text.

Or, the correct selector might be:

error_message = page.locator(’[data-test=“error”]’)

But Playwright supports multiple ways of selecting, such as using the data-testid attribute, so when writing the code you need to verify the correct way of locating elements.

So a possibly better way is to use the data-test attribute to select elements—for example, the data-test attributes on the login page:

Username input: data-test=“username”

Password input: data-test=“password”

Login button: data-test=“login-button”

Error-message element: data-test=“error”, so its element can be located as:

self.error_message = page.locator(’[data-test=“error”]’)

Then its text content can be obtained with error_message.inner_text(), which contains the key part of the error message.

As for the other pages, such as the inventory page and the cart page:

InventoryPage may have a method for adding a product to the cart, a method for navigating to the cart, and perhaps a display of the cart count. For example:

class InventoryPage: def init(self, page: Page): self.page = page

def add_product_to_cart(self, product_name): # Here we assume how the add button corresponding to the product name is located; suppose the data-test attribute has a corresponding add-to-cart button, e.g. data-test=“add-to-cart-sauce-labs-backpack” product_id = product_name.lower().replace(’ ‘, ‘-’) self.page.locator(f’[data-test=“add-to-cart-{product_id}”]’).click()

def get_cart_count(self): return self.page.locator(’.shopping_cart_badge’).inner_text()

The CartPage class may have a checkout button:

class CartPage: def init(self, page: Page): self.page = page

The CheckoutPage class:

class CheckoutPage: def init(self, page: Page): self.page = page self.first_name_input = page.locator(’[data-test=“firstName”]’) self.last_name_input = page.locator(’[data-test=“lastName”]’) self.postal_code_input = page.locator(’[data-test=“postalCode”]’) self.continue_button = page.locator(’[data-test=“continue”]’) self.error_message = page.locator(’[data-test=“error”]’)

Then, on the page after the information is filled in, there may be a finish button, in the CheckoutOverviewPage class:

class CheckoutOverviewPage: def init(self, page: Page): self.page = page self.finish_button = page.locator(’[data-test=“finish”]’) self.confirmation_message = page.locator(’.complete-header’)

In this way, the overall test flow can be chained together through the methods of each page.

Now the steps for writing the test cases:

Testing the login flow:

Parametrize different user data and determine whether login succeeds, or whether the correct error prompt appears.

For example:

In test_login.py:

import pytest from playwright.sync_api import Page

@pytest.mark.parametrize(“user_key, expected_success, expected_error”, [ (“valid_user”, True, None), (“invalid_password_user”, False, “Epic sadface: Username and password do not match”), (“locked_user”, False, “Epic sadface: Sorry, this user has been locked out.”), (“missing_username”, False, “Epic sadface: Username is required”), (“missing_password”, False, “Epic sadface: Password is required”), ]) def test_login(login_page, user_key, expected_success, expected_error): # Load user data from YAML; assume there is a fixture that can load all the test user data users = load_users() user = users[user_key] login_page.navigate() login_page.login(user[‘username’], user[‘password’])

if expected_success: assert login_page.page.url == “https://www.saucedemo.com/inventory.html" else: assert login_page.get_error_message() == expected_error

The load_users function needs to be written, or a fixture used to pass data to the test cases.

Here load_users might be a fixture in conftest.py:

import pytest import yaml

@pytest.fixture def users(): with open(‘user.yml’) as f: data = yaml.safe_load(f) return data[‘users’]

Then the test case can receive users as a fixture:

def test_login(login_page, users, user_key, expected_success, …): user = users[user_key] …

But this kind of parametrization may need to be combined with the use of indirect parameters, or the user data may need to be obtained dynamically during parametrization.

Or, map the parametrized data to the user keys and obtain the correct user data through a dictionary.

This may require a deeper handling of pytest’s parametrization, such as using indirect parametrization, passing the user key as a parameter, and then obtaining the corresponding user’s data inside the test function.

Or, this way of passing parameters may not be very straightforward, and the parametrization structure may need to be redesigned.

Perhaps the best way is to directly specify the keys of the user data in the parametrization list, and then use that key in the test case to index the corresponding data in the users fixture.

For example:

@pytest.mark.parametrize(“user_key, expected_success, expected_error”, [ (“valid_user”, True, None), (“invalid_password_user”, False, “Epic sadface: Username and password do not match”), (“locked_user”, False, “Epic sadface: Sorry, this user has been locked out.”), (“missing_username”, False, “Epic sadface: Username is required”), (“missing_password”, False, “Epic sadface: Password is required”), ]) def test_login(login_page, users, user_key, expected_success, expected_error): user = users[user_key] login_page.navigate() login_page.login(user[‘username’], user[‘password’]) if expected_success: assert login_page.page.url == “https://www.saucedemo.com/inventory.html" else: assert login_page.get_error_message() == expected_error

It needs to be ensured that the corresponding keys exist in user.yml and that the data for each user is correct.

For the normal test of the checkout flow:

In test_checkout.py:

def test_successful_checkout(login_page, inventory_page, users): valid_user = users[‘valid_user’] login_page.login(valid_user[‘username’], valid_user[‘password’]) inventory_page.add_product_to_cart(“Sauce Labs Backpack”) cart_page = inventory_page.go_to_cart() checkout_page = cart_page.checkout() checkout_page.fill_shipping_info(“John”, “Doe”, “12345”) checkout_page.continue_to_overview() overview_page = CheckoutOverviewPage(checkout_page.page) overview_page.finish_checkout() assert overview_page.get_confirmation_message() == “Thank you for your order!”

This requires defining the corresponding elements and methods of the CheckoutOverviewPage class.

For exceptional tests:

For example, omitting a required field when filling in the information:

@pytest.mark.parametrize(“first_name, last_name, zip_code, expected_error”, [ (””, “Doe”, “12345”, “Error: First Name is required”), (“John”, “”, “12345”, “Error: Last Name is required”), (“John”, “Doe”, “”, “Error: Postal Code is required”), ]) def test_checkout_error_messages(login_page, inventory_page, users, first_name, last_name, zip_code, expected_error): valid_user = users[‘valid_user’] login_page.login(valid_user[‘username’], valid_user[‘password’]) inventory_page.add_product_to_cart(“Sauce Labs Backpack”) cart_page = inventory_page.go_to_cart() checkout_page = cart_page.checkout() checkout_page.fill_shipping_info(first_name, last_name, zip_code) checkout_page.continue_to_overview() assert checkout_page.get_error_message() == expected_error

Here, it needs to be confirmed whether the actual error prompt is text like this. For example, on the reqreal site, when the first name is left blank and you continue, whether the error prompt is really “Error: First Name is required”. The actual page needs to be examined—perhaps whether the error message is contained in a data-test=“error” element, or whether it is some other structure.

In summary, the whole project needs:

  • Correctly configure each page class of the POM.
  • Correctly read the user data and parametrize the test cases.
  • Handle the flows of different test scenarios, especially that the Test checkout flow may require continuous page navigation and state maintenance.
  • Assert on exceptional cases, such as the correctness of error messages.

It may also be necessary to confirm the synchronization of page elements. Although Playwright waits automatically, for example, confirming certain elements on the page to check whether the navigation after clicking a button has completed may make things more stable.

Key Points and Explanation

  1. POM Design Pattern:

    • Each page (such as the login page or the inventory page) is encapsulated as a class, with page elements and operations abstracted into methods, thereby improving code reusability and maintainability.

  2. Data-Driven Testing:

    • User data is separated from the test code and stored in a YAML file, which improves maintainability and makes it easy to add new test scenarios.

  3. Exceptional Scenario Coverage:

    • Parametrized tests verify whether different erroneous inputs (such as a locked user, a wrong password, or a missing required field) trigger the correct error prompt.

  4. Fixture Management:

    • pytest fixtures are used to manage the browser and page objects, ensuring the independence of each test case and reducing duplicate code.

  5. Playwright Auto-Waiting Mechanism:

    • Playwright’s built-in auto-waiting ensures that elements are in an interactable state before being operated on, enhancing test stability.

This solution covers both normal and exceptional business flows, ensuring automated verification of the core functional points (login, cart, checkout) and improving software quality.

The hottest technology today is undoubtedly OpenAI’s ChatGPT, and AI technology has been widely applied in many areas. Today we’ll discuss TestGPT, a popular application in the software testing field.

What is TestGPT?

TestGPT is an artificial intelligence model (AI model) for the testing domain, released by CodiumAI Ltd., a startup company headquartered in Tel Aviv, Israel. It is powered by OpenAI’s GPT-4 large language model.

Official website: www.codium.ai

From the website’s introduction, it’s clear that TestGPT is an AI tool designed to assist developers in testing their code, providing automatically generated software test suite suggestions to accelerate coding and error scanning.

How to Use It?

Currently, TestGPT offers plugin support for VsCode and JetBrains

Taking VsCode as an example, you can install it by searching for CodiumAI in the VsCode extension marketplace

After installation, you can log in directly with your Github account.

Switch to the CodiumAI plugin, and after connecting, you can see that the code section already has an entry point for generating tests

Try generating tests and see the effect. After a moment, you can see the AI’s results

The AI assistant interface has three parts:

  • Test Suite
  • Code Analysis
  • Code Suggestions

In the test configuration section, you can make basic test configurations

The Coverage section shows the coverage of the AI-generated cases

The Test section contains the specific test cases. In this example, 6 test cases were generated

After execution, you can see the test results, but all the generated test code executed successfully, seemingly not detecting the bug through the test code :(

Code Analysis provides an analytical explanation of the code

The Code Suggestions section provides modification suggestions, which accurately points out the problem in the code.

Applying the suggestion directly, you can see that the code has been modified and comments have been added

Conclusion

So we can see that TestGPT is indeed excellent, accurately analyzing the purpose of the code and identifying problematic areas. It also helps design test case coverage and related unit test scripts. Making good use of this tool can undoubtedly provide great assistance to development engineers. However, from initial use, the self-generated test cases still have deficiencies in covering problematic code, and in the short term, it’s probably not sufficient to replace test design.
